section.title: They Have Afflicted Me from My Youth
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents, tenth in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Israel looks back over her long history of affliction, from Egypt onward, and confesses that though deeply wounded, she has never been destroyed, because the LORD Himself has cut her free.
section.thesis: Israel's long history of affliction has left real scars, yet the LORD's righteousness has kept His people from being overcome and will bring lasting shame on those who hate Zion, a pattern of suffering followed by vindication fulfilled in Christ's own affliction and triumph.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the long history of affliction survived, verses 1 to 3, the LORD's righteous deliverance, verse 4, and the closing prayer that the enemies of Zion would wither in shame, verses 5 to 8.

units.label: They have not prevailed against me

verses.text: Many a time they have persecuted me from my youth, let Israel now declare,
many a time they have persecuted me from my youth, but they have not prevailed against me.
The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long.

units.label: He has cut me from the cords of the wicked

verses.text: The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the {{avoth|cords}} of the wicked.

units.label: May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame

verses.text: May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame.
May they be like grass on the rooftops, which withers before it can grow,
unable to fill the hands of the reaper, or the arms of the binder of sheaves.
May none who pass by say to them, "The blessing of the LORD be on you; we bless you in the name of the LORD."

avoth.gloss: Cords, ropes, or thick bindings, used elsewhere for a yoke's harness; the LORD's righteousness is shown precisely in cutting the cords that bound His people to the wicked, verse 4.

basic.context: This Song of Ascents rehearses Israel's long history of affliction, from the persecution of her youth in Egypt onward, and confesses that despite deep, real wounds, she has survived because the LORD is righteous and has cut her free, then prays that those who hate Zion would wither like shallow rooftop grass.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes Israel's national history of survived affliction and it prescribes as an abiding pattern honest acknowledgment of real suffering alongside confident trust in the LORD's righteous deliverance and prayer for the ultimate defeat of His people's enemies.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm turns on avoth, cords or bindings, cut by the LORD in verse 4, the vivid image of a yoke or rope of bondage snapped by His righteous intervention, freeing His afflicted people.
basic.typology: The plowed back of Israel anticipates the scourging of Christ, and the declaration 'they have not prevailed' anticipates His resurrection victory over every power that sought to destroy Him.
basic.christ: Jesus was scourged before His crucifixion, John 19:1, His back plowed as Israel's was, yet death did not prevail against Him, and at the cross He decisively cut the cords of sin, death, and the devil that bound His people, disarming every hostile power, Colossians 2:15.
basic.god: The LORD is righteous, and His righteousness is displayed precisely in cutting the cords of the wicked that bind His afflicted people, delivering them not because they deserved it but because He is faithful to His covenant.
basic.crossReferences: John 19:1 shows Jesus scourged, His back plowed as Israel's was, prior to His victorious resurrection. Colossians 2:15 shows Christ disarming rulers and authorities, cutting every binding cord of sin and death. Romans 8:37 declares believers more than conquerors through Him who loved them.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's pattern of long affliction followed by the LORD's righteous deliverance is fulfilled in Christ, scourged and afflicted yet never overcome, who cuts the cords of sin and death for His people and secures their final victory over every enemy.

context.literary:
The psalm is a small drama in three scenes, and it is built to be sung by a crowd. Verse 1 ends with a summons, 'let Israel now declare', and the whole congregation is cued to take up the line in verse 2. The first line is therefore sung twice, once by a leader and once by the people, and the repetition is a form of testimony. The same call appears in Psalm 124:1 and in Psalm 118:2, where 'Let Israel say' opens a liturgy of thanks.

The first scene, verses 1 to 3, is a memory of suffering. Its details are bodily: a back, and furrows cut into it by men with a plough. The middle verse, 2, is the turn. After 'many a time they have persecuted me from my youth' comes the single clause that carries the rest, 'but they have not prevailed against me'. The sentence says the same thing twice and then takes a turn at the end, and the turn is the point.

The second scene is one verse, and it is the centre of the psalm. 'The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked', verse 4. Everything before it is endurance, and everything after it is prayer. The psalm turns on what God has done, and on His character, righteous, as the reason.

The third scene, verses 5 to 8, is a prayer in the form of a wish. It is built around a single image, a plant that fails, and the images keep the farming language of the first scene. The plough of verse 3 and the sheaves of verse 7 belong to one field. The enemies, who made furrows on Israel's back, are themselves sown on a roof where nothing can grow and no reaper can gather a handful. The psalm ends with the withholding of a blessing, which is an unusual ending for a pilgrim song, and the next psalm leaves the field for the depths.
context.historical:
The psalm says 'from my youth', and the Old Testament uses youth of Israel's beginnings in Egypt. 'When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son', Hosea 11:1, and Hosea 2:15 speaks of 'the days of her youth, as in the day she came up out of Egypt'. The first persecution in the national memory is the new king who 'did not know Joseph' and set taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them, Exodus 1:8 to 14. That passage also records the strange fact that the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied, Exodus 1:12, which is the psalm's 'they have not prevailed' told in a verse.

The centuries that followed supplied more hostility. Israel's later history includes the attacks of neighbouring peoples, the Assyrian invasions and the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon. Psalm 83:3 and 4 shows the sentiment: 'Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more'. The speaker of Psalm 129 is a single 'I', and in the Songs of Ascents that 'I' is the pilgrim who stands for the whole people.

The farming imagery would have been plain to hearers. A plough in the ancient Near East was a wooden tool drawn by a team of oxen, and long furrows could run the length of a field. To picture one's back as ploughed ground is to picture a body treated as soil. Isaiah describes Jerusalem in the same terms, as a people who made their backs 'like the ground, like a street to be traversed', Isaiah 51:23. Micah had foretold that 'Zion will be plowed like a field', Micah 3:12, and Jeremiah 26:18 recalls the saying, so the language of ploughing Zion was part of Israel's tragic vocabulary.

The rooftop was part of the house. Roofs in Palestine were flat and covered with packed earth or plaster, and windblown seed could sprout on them in the rains and die as soon as the sun came out, since the soil was thin. Everyone knew grass of this kind. It is the same image used of the Assyrians' victims in 2 Kings 19:26, 'grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown'.

The final verse reflects a custom of harvest greeting. When Boaz came to his reapers he said 'The LORD be with you', and they answered 'The LORD bless you', Ruth 2:4. The psalm has the passerby withhold that courtesy from the enemies of Zion, which is a social snub and also a theological verdict.
context.canonical:
The psalm belongs with the other songs in which the LORD's people recite what they have survived. Psalm 124 does it in the first person plural, with the same opening formula, 'If the LORD had not been on our side', and ends with a bird escaped from the fowler's snare, 'the net is torn, and we have slipped away', Psalm 124:7. Psalm 129 shares its theme with the neighbouring Psalm 125, 'As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people', Psalm 125:2, and it has something in common with Psalm 126, where the harvest is joy, and Psalm 127, where building is vain without the LORD.

The word 'prevail' recalls Israel's own name. When Jacob wrestled he was told 'you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed', Genesis 32:28, and the same root of strength and ability is in the psalm's 'they have not prevailed'. A people named for prevailing now sings that their enemies have not. The word returns in God's word to Jeremiah, 'They will fight against you but will never overcome you, since I am with you to deliver you', Jeremiah 1:19.

Cutting cords belongs to the language of deliverance. 'Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords', say the rebels in Psalm 2:3, and the LORD, who liberates, says in Isaiah 58:6 that He wants His people 'to untie the cords of the yoke' and to 'set the oppressed free'. In Hosea 11:4 He describes His own leading as 'cords of kindness, with ropes of love', and speaks of lifting the yoke from their necks. The cords in Psalm 129:4 belong to the wicked, but the same word can describe the cords of God's own love.

The New Testament takes the psalm's confidence into the church. Jesus says 'the gates of Hades will not prevail against it', Matthew 16:18. Paul writes 'persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed', 2 Corinthians 4:9, and in Romans 8:35 to 37 asks whether persecution can separate believers from Christ's love, and answers that in all these things they are more than conquerors. The risen Christ identifies with His persecuted people when He asks Saul, 'why do you persecute Me?', Acts 9:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm trains a persecuted people to tell their history in the right order. The wounds come first and are named without softening, for the psalmist does not say the suffering was small. The order matters, though: the congregation is told to say that they were afflicted and that they were not prevailed against, in one breath, and to say it together.

The author's point is that survival is evidence of something. A small people with a long history of enemies is still here, and the explanation is not their strength. The psalm names the reason in verse 4, the righteousness of the LORD. His character, not Israel's resilience, is what cut the cords. The first hearers are being taught to read their own survival as a testimony to Him.

The closing prayer expresses a longing that evil will not flourish where God's people live. The imagery of wilting grass is not a call to violence but a request that the enemies of Zion bear no fruit, that their schemes will come to nothing. The psalm asks the LORD to deal with those who hate His people and His city, and it leaves the matter in His hands. The people are meant to go up to Zion with their grief told and their cause committed to the righteous LORD.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first half is description, an account of what happened to Israel. Nothing in it tells believers to seek suffering or to accept every kind of abuse as God's will. The plough is a picture of what was done to Israel, and it is told as grief.

The second half is a prayer, and prayers record what a believer may say to God, not what he must do to others. The words 'May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame' are addressed to the LORD. The psalm does not tell anyone to carry out its wish. Elsewhere Scripture is clear that vengeance belongs to God, and Paul says 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath', Romans 12:19. The prayer is an example of how to hand an injustice over.

What carries forward is a way of speaking to God in persecution: remembering what has been survived, naming the wrong, confessing His righteousness and committing the enemy to Him. The psalm's wish for shame is best read alongside Jesus' command to love enemies and pray for those who persecute, Matthew 5:44, and Paul's command to bless those who persecute, Romans 12:14. The two do not cancel each other. The believer prays that evil will fail and that the evildoer will repent.

debates.question: How should Christians pray the wishes of verses 5 to 8?

views.label: As a prayer for God's justice against persistent evil
views.case: The psalm does not say 'let us shame them' but 'may they be turned back'. It hands the matter to God and asks Him to defeat those who hate Zion. Scripture treats such prayers as legitimate, as in Psalm 35:4 and Revelation 6:9 and 10, where the martyrs ask how long until justice comes. The prayer expresses a longing that evil should not win.

views.label: As a prayer to be shaped by Christ's command to love enemies
views.case: Jesus said 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you', Matthew 5:44, and from the cross prayed 'Father, forgive them', Luke 23:34. On this reading the believer prays the psalm's substance, that the plans of evil fail, while praying that the persecutor will be turned back by repentance rather than by ruin.

debates.bearing: The two views fit together. Paul commands both leaving vengeance to God and blessing persecutors, Romans 12:14 and 19 to 21. A believer can ask God to stop the persecution of His people and to turn the persecutor, and Saul, who persecuted the church and was stopped on the road, Acts 9:4, is the best example of the second prayer being answered.

debates.question: Who is the 'me' who has been persecuted from youth, and when was that youth?

views.label: The nation Israel, from Egypt onward
views.case: The summons to Israel in verse 1 makes the speaker the whole people. Hosea speaks of Israel's youth as the time of the exodus, Hosea 11:1, and the first oppression was in Egypt, Exodus 1. The singular speaks for a people as one body.

views.label: The individual pilgrim, with the nation behind him
views.case: Pilgrim psalms are sung by individuals, and the 'I' of the Ascents is often personal, as in Psalm 120:1 and Psalm 122:1. Each singer takes the national story as his own, and the verses become both a nation's and a person's testimony.

debates.bearing: The call to Israel in verse 1 makes the psalm corporate, and the singular makes it personal. Both are true when each pilgrim sings, which is why the church can sing it of the body of Christ and of each believer.

study.originalLanguages:
The word translated 'many a time' in verses 1 and 2 is rabbat, which has the sense of 'much' or 'abundantly', and is used here as an adverb. The sense is of a long, heavy history, not only a number of events. 'From my youth' uses the word for young life, from the same family as the word Hosea uses of Israel's early days in Hosea 2:15. The refrain is repeated word for word in verse 2, and the first line is a refrain that the people sing back.

The verb for 'persecuted' in verses 1 and 2 means to bind, press or show hostility to, from a root that describes tightness and affliction, and it is related to the word for 'enemy' and 'trouble'. It names a hostility that confines. The effect on the ear is a chain of narrowing words, set against the verb 'prevail', which opens a way through.

'They have not prevailed' uses the verb yakol, 'to be able' or 'to overcome', the same root as in Genesis 32:28 where Jacob is told he has prevailed, and Jeremiah 1:19, 'will never overcome you'. The sentence uses a word for ability and power in the negative. The BSB renders the forceful phrase as 'not prevailed against me', and the psalm means that their efforts did not reach the goal of destroying Israel.

The verb of ploughing, charash, describes the driving of a plough, and the noun for the 'plowmen' shares the root. The verse says they ploughed 'upon my back' and 'lengthened their furrows'. The verb for 'long' is the one that means to make long, drawn out, as in a long run of furrow. The picture is of a long and relentless cutting. The same consonants in the verb charash can also mean to devise or plot, as in Proverbs 3:29, so some hear a pun of ploughing and plotting, though the psalm's picture does not depend on it.

In verse 4 the verb is qitstsets, 'to cut' or 'cut off', in an intensive pattern, and the noun is avoth, 'cords' or 'ropes'. The avoth are thick braided cords, the sort used to bind a prisoner, as Samson was bound, Judges 15:13, or to harness an animal, and the same word appears in Psalm 2:3 and Hosea 11:4. The righteous one cuts them with a single stroke, and the verse offers no human actor. 'Righteous', tsaddiq, is the word that Pharaoh himself uses of the LORD after the plague of hail, Exodus 9:27, and it is a title of His covenant faithfulness, Psalm 116:5.

In verse 6 the 'grass on the rooftops' is chatsir gaggot, the same phrase as in 2 Kings 19:26, and the final clause of the verse is ambiguous. The BSB reads 'withers before it can grow', and the verb behind it can also mean to draw out or pull up, so that the grass is plucked before it matures. Both give the picture of a plant with no future.

typology.fulfillment: Israel's back plowed by oppressors is a pattern of the suffering of God's people at the hands of the powers. Isaiah's Servant says 'I offered My back to those who struck Me', Isaiah 50:6, and the Gospels record that Pilate 'had Jesus flogged', John 19:1 and Mark 15:15. Peter says 'By His stripes you are healed', 1 Peter 2:24, which echoes Isaiah 53:5. Christ is at once the faithful Israel who suffers and the Son who bears the suffering for others. The type falls short because Israel's wounds were the result of oppression, while Christ's were taken voluntarily and carried sin.

typology.type: The cords cut by the LORD, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: The cutting of the cords is a picture of release from bondage, such as the exodus, when the LORD brought Israel out from under the yoke of the Egyptians, Exodus 6:6. At the cross Christ cancelled the record of debt against us, nailed it to the cross and disarmed the powers, Colossians 2:14 and 15, and by His death freed those held in slavery by fear of death, Hebrews 2:14 and 15. The type is partial, because Israel was freed from a human oppressor, while believers are freed from sin, death and the devil.

typology.type: 'They have not prevailed against me', verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The refrain finds its sharpest instance in the resurrection. Jesus was put to death by the hands of the lawless, but God raised Him, 'because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches', Acts 2:23 and 24. Death did its worst and did not prevail. The church shares the pattern, since Jesus promises that the gates of Hades will not prevail against the church, Matthew 16:18. The type is limited because Israel's survival was preservation through suffering, while Christ's was victory through death.

typology.type: Grass on the rooftops, verses 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The withering of the enemies is a picture of the end of the powers that oppose God. Isaiah says the grass withers but the word of God stands forever, Isaiah 40:7 and 8. In the New Testament the ultimate enemy, death, is destroyed by Christ, 1 Corinthians 15:26, and the rulers of this age are coming to nothing, 1 Corinthians 2:6. The type is incomplete since it describes the failure of human schemes, while the New Testament looks to a final judgement by the Lord, Revelation 20:10 to 15.

study.christ:
The psalm speaks of a back that was ploughed and of a persecuted one who was not prevailed against, and the Gospels point to Jesus on both counts. John writes that Pilate took Jesus and had Him flogged, John 19:1, and Isaiah's Servant, whom the church has always read as a portrait of Jesus, says 'I offered My back to those who struck Me', Isaiah 50:6. Peter says that when He was abused 'He did not retaliate', but entrusted Himself to the one who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. The righteous sufferer of the psalm has become the righteous one who bore the flogging.

The second half of the verse, 'they have not prevailed', is realised in the empty tomb. Peter tells the crowd at Pentecost that they put Jesus to death by nailing Him to the cross, 'But God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches', Acts 2:23 and 24. The enemies did their worst, and the worst did not prevail.

The cutting of cords is what He did on the cross. Paul says that God, having cancelled the debt ascribed to us, took it away, 'nailing it to the cross', and 'having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross', Colossians 2:14 and 15. The Hebrews writer says that by His death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death and free those held in slavery by fear of it, Hebrews 2:14 and 15. The righteous LORD of verse 4 acts in His Son.

There is a further link in the identity of the sufferer. When Saul persecuted the church, the risen Lord asked him, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?', Acts 9:4. Jesus counts the persecution of His people as persecution of Himself, and says to them 'If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well', John 15:20. The 'me' of the psalm, the persecuted community, is the body of the one who was persecuted and raised. Their survival is part of His victory, and Paul draws the conclusion that in all their sufferings they are 'more than conquerors through Him who loved us', Romans 8:37.

As for the prayer against the haters of Zion, the New Testament shows how Christ answers it. He bids His followers pray for their persecutors, Matthew 5:44, and prays for His own executioners, Luke 23:34, and yet He is also the judge who will deal with evil in the end. The psalm's wish that the enemies bear no fruit is answered both in the conversion of persecutors like Saul and in the final defeat of the powers.

A caution is needed. The psalm is about Israel's national experience and does not mention a coming Messiah. The links above are those the New Testament makes in its own words, and every detail of the plough should not be forced into a prophecy of the cross.
study.god:
The psalm's one theological sentence is 'The LORD is righteous', and everything else in it hangs on that. Righteous here means more than fair. It names His faithfulness to what He has promised and to the people He has bound Himself to. He is the God who acts rightly toward the wronged. When His people have suffered for centuries, the psalm's claim is that He has not been indifferent, for He is the one who cut the cords.

He is the one who preserves a people through history. The psalm credits Israel's survival to Him, not to its own strength, and the pattern runs through the book of Exodus, in which the more they were oppressed the more they multiplied, Exodus 1:12. Psalm 124 says it directly: if the LORD had not been on our side, they would have swallowed us alive, Psalm 124:1 to 3. His faithfulness works through time and across generations.

He is also a God who lets affliction come before He delivers. The psalm does not say that the plough did not cut. It says the furrows were long. He did not prevent the suffering, and the psalm does not explain why. It gives instead a confession of His character in the middle of the suffering. That is a form of trust that does not require the questions to be answered first.

He is a God of justice who takes up the cause of Zion. The prayer of verses 5 to 8 asks Him to turn back those who hate it, and the shape of the prayer, withering and fruitlessness, places the judgement in His hands. Israel's God is not partisan for the sake of a nation. He is the one who promised Abraham 'I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you', Genesis 12:3, and the psalm's last verse is the human side of that promise: blessing is withheld from those who stand against what He has done.

He is a God who blesses and who can withhold blessing. The ending of the psalm turns on a greeting. The blessing of the LORD is not an empty courtesy. It is something He gives, and those who set themselves against His people are not covered by it. The seriousness of this is balanced elsewhere by the word of the New Testament that He desires everyone to come to repentance, 2 Peter 3:9.

For worship, the psalm teaches a congregation to tell the story of its suffering aloud, with the line 'He has cut me from the cords of the wicked' as the centre. It teaches that praise can sit beside a history of pain, and that lament and trust belong in the same song.

crossReferences.note: The first oppression in Israel's memory: a king who did not know Joseph, forced labour in brick and mortar, and harsh service in the fields. The verses also record that the more they were oppressed, the more they flourished, which is the 'they have not prevailed' of the psalm told as history.

Another Song of Ascents with the same call, 'let Israel now declare', and the same theme: Israel survived because the LORD was on its side. It ends with the net torn and the bird freed, a close companion to the cutting of the cords in Psalm 129:4.

Jacob is renamed Israel because he has struggled with God and with men and has prevailed. The same root of prevailing is in the psalm's denial that the enemies prevailed, so that the nation's very name is behind the confession that they cannot overcome it.

The LORD says that the cup of His fury will pass to Israel's tormentors, who told His people to lie down so they could walk over them, so that they made their backs like the ground. It shows the same image as verse 3 in a prophet's words, with the promise that the oppressor will pay.

The prophet warns that Zion will be plowed like a field. The psalm's ploughing of Israel's back and Micah's ploughing of Zion belong to the same tragic vocabulary, in which God's people and city are treated as soil by the powers, and yet are not destroyed.

In the Assyrian crisis the LORD describes the inhabitants of conquered cities as grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown. The phrase is the same as in Psalm 129:6, and it shows that the image of useless, short-lived grass was applied to the powers that once threatened Jerusalem.

Boaz greets the harvesters with 'The LORD be with you', and they answer 'The LORD bless you'. This is the greeting that verse 8 has the passerby withhold from the enemies of Zion. It shows the ordinary, warm harvest custom against which the psalm's last line is a sharp refusal.

Paul tells believers to bless those who persecute them and not to avenge themselves, leaving room for God's wrath, and to overcome evil with good. It is the New Testament guide to praying a psalm like this one: committing the wrong to God and hoping for the persecutor's good.

God made believers alive with Christ, cancelled the debt against them, nailed it to the cross and disarmed the powers and authorities, triumphing over them. It is the New Testament account of the cutting of the cords, the deliverance of a people from every bondage by a single act of the righteous LORD.

Paul describes the apostles as hard pressed but not crushed, persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed. It is the experience of Psalm 129 in the life of the church, where the affliction is real and the survival is the work of God.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story has an enemy from its third chapter. When God promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head, Genesis 3:15, He announces that there will be a long conflict between the line of promise and the powers that oppose it. Psalm 129 is a song from the middle of that conflict. Israel is the seed that keeps being struck and keeps surviving, and the psalm is its testimony.

The pattern begins in Egypt and recurs. Pharaoh seeks to destroy the people through labour and the killing of their sons, Exodus 1, and the LORD brings them out. In later centuries the same pattern appears in Assyria, Babylon and the nations that sought to erase the name of Israel, Psalm 83:4. Each time the people survive. The exile looks like a defeat, and the return is a resurrection of sorts, Psalm 126. The preservation of Israel is a thread that keeps the line of promise unbroken until the Messiah.

In Christ the conflict reaches its centre. The enemy strikes the Seed Himself, the back is ploughed, the body is nailed to a tree, and the powers believe they have prevailed. Yet it is impossible for death to hold Him, Acts 2:24. At the cross the cords are cut and the powers disarmed, Colossians 2:15. The church, joined to Him, goes on to suffer and survive, 2 Corinthians 4:8 and 9, and learns that the gates of Hades will not prevail against it, Matthew 16:18.

The prayer against the haters of Zion looks to the end. The powers that oppose God's people are like grass that withers, Isaiah 40:7 and 8, and the book of Revelation shows the last enemies defeated, Revelation 20:10 and 14. The martyrs' cry 'How long?', Revelation 6:10, is answered when the Lord judges, and the blessing that the psalm withholds from the enemies is given in full to His people.

The new creation has no plough on any back. There is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and nothing impure can enter the city, Revelation 21:27. The persecuted people who sang 'Many a time they have persecuted me from my youth' will sing a new song before the throne, and the testimony of Psalm 129 will be told as finished history: they did not prevail.

sermon.title: That's Life!
sermon.why: Begg treats Psalms 129 to 131 together, showing how this psalm's honest reckoning with long affliction leads into the trust and humility of the psalms that follow.

quiz.q: What does Israel declare in verses 1 to 2 about her long history of persecution?

options.text: Many times she has been persecuted from her youth, yet enemies have not prevailed against her.
options.note: This is the exact double declaration of the opening verses.

options.text: She has never once faced any persecution.
options.note: The psalm explicitly describes repeated, long-standing persecution, not its absence.

options.text: Her enemies eventually destroyed her completely.
options.note: The psalm insists the opposite, that enemies have not prevailed.

options.text: She has only faced persecution in recent memory.
options.note: The phrase 'from my youth' points to a very long, ongoing history, not merely recent events.

quiz.q: What image does verse 3 use to describe the suffering Israel endured?

options.text: Plowmen plowing over her back, making long furrows.
options.note: This vivid, painful image is the exact picture the psalm uses for deep, real suffering.

options.text: A gentle breeze passing over a field.
options.note: The image is one of deep, painful wounding, not something gentle or mild.

options.text: A brief shadow that quickly passed.
options.note: The furrows are described as long, suggesting sustained and severe suffering, not a brief shadow.

options.text: A minor scratch quickly healed.
options.note: The imagery of plowed furrows suggests deep, lasting wounds, not a minor injury.

quiz.q: What does verse 4 say the LORD has done?

options.text: Being righteous, He has cut Israel free from the cords of the wicked.
options.note: This is the psalm's turning point, crediting Israel's deliverance to the LORD's righteous act.

options.text: He has ignored Israel's suffering entirely.
options.note: The verse credits the LORD directly with decisive, righteous deliverance.

options.text: He has increased the cords binding Israel to her enemies.
options.note: The verse describes the LORD cutting, not increasing, the cords of bondage.

options.text: He has delayed any response for centuries.
options.note: The verse presents the LORD's righteous action as decisive, not as an indefinite delay.

quiz.q: What does the psalm pray will happen to those who hate Zion, according to verses 5 to 7?

options.text: That they be turned back in shame, like rooftop grass that withers before it can grow.
options.note: This is the exact imprecatory prayer and imagery of the closing verses.

options.text: That they would prosper and multiply endlessly.
options.note: The prayer is for their shame and fruitlessness, the opposite of prosperity.

options.text: That they would be given a permanent alliance with Israel.
options.note: The prayer is for their defeat and shame, not for alliance or partnership.

options.text: That they would receive a slow, gradual decline over centuries.
options.note: The image of rooftop grass withering 'before it can grow' suggests a swift, not slow, futility.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's pattern of affliction followed by deliverance find fulfillment in Christ?

options.text: Jesus was scourged like Israel's plowed back, yet death did not prevail against Him, and He disarmed every hostile power at the cross.
options.note: John 19:1 and Colossians 2:15 show this exact pattern fulfilled decisively in Christ.

options.text: Christ avoided all suffering entirely.
options.note: The New Testament clearly describes Christ's real suffering, including scourging before crucifixion.

options.text: Christ's suffering ended in permanent defeat with no vindication.
options.note: The resurrection is the decisive vindication that answers His suffering, the opposite of permanent defeat.

options.text: The pattern applies only to ancient Israel and has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The New Testament draws a direct line from this pattern of affliction and deliverance to Christ's own suffering and victory.

questions: The psalm honestly names deep, long-standing suffering, plowed furrows on the back, without denying its reality. Where do you need to bring honest lament, rather than forced positivity, before God this week?
Despite real affliction, Israel confesses 'they have not prevailed against me.' What battle in your life feels ongoing, and how does this psalm's confidence in ultimate survival encourage you?
The LORD's righteousness is shown in cutting the cords of the wicked. What binding sin, fear, or circumstance do you need Christ to cut you free from right now?

The psalm prays for the shame and fruitlessness of those who hate Zion, echoing Christ's call to also pray for enemies' repentance. How can you pray for God's justice while also longing for your opponents' salvation?

Christ's own scourged back and ultimate resurrection victory fulfill this psalm's pattern. How does knowing that Jesus endured worse affliction than you, and triumphed, strengthen your endurance today?

translationNotes.note: Many a time can also be rendered often or repeatedly, emphasizing the recurring, not singular, nature of Israel's persecution across her history.
The image of plowmen plowing over the back reflects ancient Near Eastern scourging practices, turning the language of agriculture into a picture of severe physical suffering.
Grass on the rooftops grew in the thin layer of soil on flat Middle Eastern roofs, sprouting quickly after rain but withering just as fast in the sun, an image of shallow, short-lived futility.
